item.title: Autism, Masking, and the Pursuit of Happiness
item.description:
Autism

Autism, Masking, and the Pursuit of Happiness

Exploring strategies to help autistic individuals unmask and live authentically.

Posted October 23, 2026

Key points
  • Masking and social camouflage are associated with short-term success and a long-term mental health impact.
  • Traditional efforts to teach social skills may encourage inadvertent masking of autistic traits.
  • Family and professionals can support autistic people by openly discussing masking and socializing options.
  • While masking can be harmful, it can also be adaptive and beneficial when used intentionally and sparingly.

As scientific investigations continue to explore and debunk suspected environmental contributors to autism, and unsubstantiated vaccine theories resurface, we risk diverting attention away from a critical public health question: How do we best support the millions of autistic children and adults living in our communities today?

For decades, autism intervention efforts have pursued a noble goal: help autistic people fit into a world that was not set up for them. Yet efforts to teach individuals “socially appropriate” behaviors have had unintended consequences. An autistic person may learn a social script, make more eye contact, or become better at navigating a conversation. On the surface, these changes look like success. But when social support becomes focused primarily on appearing less autistic, we risk teaching something else entirely – that one’s autistic identity must be actively suppressed if they want to be successful in life.

This process is commonly referred to as masking or social camouflage. It involves the act of concealing or compensating for behaviors that others perceive as socially undesirable while adopting behaviors that more closely conform to neurotypical (i.e., non-autistic) expectations.

All people engage in some degree of impression management. We monitor what we say, adjust our behavior across settings, and sometimes suppress natural impulses to achieve a social goal. Anyone who has tried to make a good impression on a first date or during a job interview understands this basic human tendency.

For autistic individuals, however, masking can become something far more pervasive. Rather than temporarily putting their best foot forward, they may feel pressure to continuously monitor their facial expressions, eye contact, body movements, tone of voice, conversational timing, disclosure of interests, and emotional reactions. In addition to completing the same school, work, and daily living responsibilities as everyone else, they must devote additional mental resources to constructing and maintaining a socially acceptable persona.

Four adolescents sitting on a brick bench and hanging out together
Source: kat wilcox / Pexels

And many become exceptionally skilled at doing so. Masking can help autistic people form personal relationships, succeed professionally, avoid bullying and peer mistreatment, and navigate myriad environments that might otherwise reject them. In this way, masking can function as an important, and arguably essential, survival strategy.

But that success comes at a cost.

Impact of Masking

Long-term masking has been associated with chronic stress, depression, anxiety, and diminished well-being. Many autistic people also describe sustained masking as directly contributing to autistic burnout–a state of profound physical, mental, and emotional exhaustion that can result in withdrawal from school, work, relationships, and other obligations. Over time, a person’s sense of identity can also become less clear. Like an actor who has played the same character for years, the boundaries between the person and the role they play can begin to blur. These challenges are especially salient among autistic people who do not realize they are masking at all. Some spend years or even decades mimicking others, rehearsing conversations, suppressing natural tendencies, and wondering why everyday social interactions seem so exhausting without understanding the reason.

If autism professionals and family members are not careful, their efforts and guidance can directly contribute to the problem. What we describe as “social skills training” can actually be training in how to hide autistic characteristics.

We need not stop providing support to autistic people, but rather, we can shift the focus of that support. Social knowledge remains tremendously valuable and even life-changing. The critical distinction is between teaching social understanding, which expands choices, and social conformity, which restricts them.

Autistic people deserve access to information about different social communication strategies and relationships, the unwritten expectations that govern social interactions, and differences in expectations across neurotypes. But that information should be offered as a set of tools and possibilities, rather than a collection of hard rules to follow.

We can begin this exploration of social topics by listening to the voices of autistic individuals themselves. What relationships do they want? What social situations are difficult for them? What is getting in the way of goals they have set for themselves? Asking these questions prevents professionals and family members from assuming that we already know what’s best for autistic individuals.

Consider Eye Contact

Traditional social skill programs have often taught autistic individuals that they should look directly into another person’s eyes during conversation. Yet eye contact can be deeply uncomfortable, distracting, and even overwhelming for some autistic people. Instead of simply instructing someone to “make eye contact,” we might instead explore why people use eye contact in the first place. Among other things, looking at another person conveys engagement and interest.

Once we understand the underlying social goal, other possibilities emerge.

A person might also convey interest by nodding along, offering a brief acknowledgement, such as “mmm-hmm” or “interesting,” sharing a related experience, asking a follow-up question, or orienting their body toward the speaker. Sure, eye contact remains a viable option, but it is no longer the only acceptable one.

This process changes the question from “How can we make this person appear more neurotypical?” to “What goal is this person trying to accomplish, and what strategies might help them do this in a way that still feels authentic?”

The Adaptive Role of Masking

When reimagining socialization support, we must also be careful to avoid demonizing masking. Masking has real practical value and remains an essential, adaptive social tool. There are situations in which an autistic person may deliberately choose to modify their behavior because doing so helps them achieve something important to them. The key word is choose.

Masking is very different when it is an intentional, strategic tool rather than an unconscious, compulsory means of navigating through the world. Autism professionals and family members both have a role in helping individuals recognize when they are masking, understand the potential benefits and costs, and decide for themselves when altering their natural behavior is worth the effort.

An autistic young adult might decide that carefully monitoring their demeanor and what they say during a job interview is worth the effort because the position matters deeply to them. That same person may decide that they do not want or need to mask while spending an evening with close friends. Neither decision is inherently right or wrong. The goal is to put that decision within the autistic person’s conscious control.

Ultimately, we must reconsider how we define success in autism support efforts. The goal of autism support should not be to teach people how to appear less autistic. It should be to help autistic people acquire tools and make decisions to build relationships, careers, communities, and lives that they themselves find personally meaningful. That is a much more worthwhile definition of social success—and a much better foundation for the pursuit of happiness.

item.title: Sex and Mental Load
item.description:
Sex

Sex and Mental Load

More stress commonly comes with less desire.

Posted October 23, 2026

Source: YuriArcursPeopleimages / Envato

This fall, a number of therapists wrote in to ask me questions on the same theme: What happens to desire when one partner is carrying a lot more of the mental load?

In a relationship, if one person is carrying significantly more of the mental load (by which I mean, keeping track of all the chores and tasks that need to happen in order to maintain a shared household), it’s pretty predictable that their desire will decrease.

Stress tends to kill desire. That’s true in acute situations — i.e., you might not feel very sexy during your most hectic and overwhelming workday. But it’s also true in more chronic, long-term situations, like when the stressors of everyday life add up to the point that sex just starts to feel like another checkbox on the to-do list.

There’s a combination of things going on here:

  • When you’re overwhelmed, it’s hard for desire to bloom.
  • If the burden of maintaining your shared life is unevenly divided, it creates resentment, which isn’t a particularly sexy feeling.
  • At the extreme end of things, one partner might end up feeling more like a caretaker or parental figure for the other partner, which can really dampen attraction.

This dynamic that arises from limited bandwidth and uneven stress or responsibility is pretty common. It can be hard to shift, particularly if…

  • communication is going sideways
  • resentment is building
  • there are differences of opinion about whether the division of labor is fair
  • power dynamics are in play
  • or one (or both!) partner(s) isn’t aware of how much heavy lifting they’ve managed to avoid

Clearly, building or maintaining a lively sexual connection requires a sense of collaboration, balance, teamwork, flexibility, and consideration, and navigating all of this can be quite complex. So, what’s a therapist to do?

  • Offer psychoeducation about stress and sex. Make sure your clients understand the relationship between sex and stress, and how chronic overwhelm with the work of running a household can dampen desire. The arousal nerves are in the parasympathetic nervous system; if you never relax, you are unlikely to be interested in getting sexual. If you’re pissed off all the time, that’s also not particularly compatible with sexual desire or arousal.
  • Take a look at different routes to relaxation. Some people use sex to down-regulate, and some can’t access sex until they down-regulate. Both of these are common. If your clients have different styles, it can be really helpful to normalize these differences, and help them have a problem-solving conversation about how to experience more togetherness.
  • Help your clients get clear on goals. My therapeutic work always starts with goals and motivation. The first step is to figure out if both partners are actually interested in having a stronger sexual connection; if not, you’re in a different conversation! But if so, the possibility of a better sex life can be powerfully motivating. For the higher-desire partner, I can’t guarantee that picking up a fairer share of the household work will lead to more sex, but it is clear that what they’ve been doing so far isn’t working. For the lower-desire partner: Are they speaking up in a calm and clear way about what they would actually love to experience sexually, intimately, and affectionately? Are they asking for the things that would help them get there?
  • Reduce the pressure around sex. That includes removing any pressure to have sex, of course, but it can also include getting more creative about how you have sex, so that there’s no pressure to engage in any one specific activity. When people assume that sex needs to include penetration, for instance, or be orgasmic for a second instance, it can feel more high-stakes and more like a chore; but sex that is focused on experiencing pleasure and connection together, in whatever form that takes, is less likely to stir up stress.

item.title: Why Emotion Regulation Is the Skill Under the Skills
item.description:
Emotion Regulation

Why Emotion Regulation Is the Skill Under the Skills

Managing feelings can be taught. The earlier kids start, the better.

Posted October 23, 2026

Key points
  • Emotion regulation is a set of learnable skills, not just something people are born with.
  • A review of 62 studies found that when therapy works, better emotion regulation is often part of the reason.
  • Therapy showed the strongest link to emotion regulation when it taught those skills directly and on purpose.
  • Kids don’t need to wait for therapy. Families, schools, and communities can teach coping skills early.

A recent car-buying experience left me thinking. When a salesperson pulled a bait-and-switch on pricing, I could feel my body react. My face got hot, my heart raced, and my voice got louder. Before things escalated further, another salesperson stepped in, staying remarkably calm, listening, and steering the conversation to a fix. That salesperson later told me that catching far more heat than I had shown was just part of the job, without a hint of defensiveness. How did that calm look so natural? Was it learned?

We often talk about emotion regulation as if it were temperament. One child is “easygoing” whereas another “has a temper.” But emotion regulation, meaning how we influence what we feel and how we express it, is not just something we are born with. It is a set of skills that includes recognizing a feeling, reflecting on it, and choosing how to respond. Coping is the part of emotion regulation that we use under stress, like taking a breath before answering an angry customer. It can be learned, with repeated opportunities to practice and get feedback, and it is consistently linked to well-being.

And new research shows these skills may matter more than we realized.

A Clue to Why Therapy Works

A team of researchers in Sweden asked a question: When therapy works, is it partly because people get better at handling their emotions? To explore the answer, they looked at 62 carefully designed studies of therapy for problems like anxiety, depression, and self-harm.

Here’s what they learned:

  • Often, the answer was yes. About half the time, learning to manage emotions was part of why therapy worked.
  • The link was strongest when it was taught on purpose. When interventions taught emotion regulation directly, using an established framework, the connection showed up about 8 out of 10 times.
  • It mattered even when it wasn’t the goal. Therapies with a different focus still seemed to work partly by building these skills.

This new research review does have limitations. Most studies can’t tell us whether emotion regulation skills improved first or people started getting better first. And every study involved people who were already struggling, mostly adults: only 10 of the 62 included kids or teens. To me, that’s the most important part of the story. If these skills help people who are already experiencing challenges, imagine what could happen if every child had the chance to learn them early.

Why Wait for Therapy? Teach Coping Early

Research with young people points in the same direction. Psychological treatments for teens and young adults with depression and anxiety reduce emotion dysregulation alongside symptoms. And skills can be taught to children at risk. For example, when children of parents with depression learned coping skills as part of a prevention program, improved coping helped explain later drops in emotional and behavioral problems.

As I wrote about in my post on youth loneliness, just as we teach children to read and write, we can also teach them to cope. But how we teach matters. In "Feel Your Best Self," for example, we guide facilitators to teach each strategy the same way: introduce it, model the steps, give time for practice, then talk and reflect together.

What Families, Schools, and Communities Can Do

The clearest lesson from the new review is to be intentional: name the skill, teach it, and practice it on purpose. That works best when families, schools, and communities share the same language and strategies, so children can practice wherever they are.

Families

  • Name feelings out loud along with what to try. “I’m frustrated. I am going to stop and try some belly breathing before I decide what to do.” Children learn the steps by hearing them.
  • Practice when calm. A coping strategy practiced in a calm moment is easier to put in place when emotions run high.
  • Treat “I need a minute” as a skill. Pausing before reacting is regulation in action. For ideas on what to do when a meltdown is underway, see my post "The Escalation Cycle."

Schools & Youth-Serving Organizations

  • Teach emotion regulation like any other skill. Choose a program that teaches coping skills, and practice a few minutes every day, as you would for reading or a free throw. Naming feelings is a start, but kids also need to explore what to do with them.
  • Use real moments to practice. Lost games, recess conflicts, and tough tests are all chances to coach a strategy in the moment, then talk about how it went afterward.
  • Support the adults, too. Teachers, coaches, and staff who can stay calm under pressure model regulation every time they do it.

Bottom Line

When therapy works, emotion regulation is often part of the reason. Children don’t have to wait that long. They can learn to recognize, reflect, and respond long before life hands them their first big test, or, in my case, a bait-and-switch tactic at a car dealership.

Disclosure: I am a co-creator of Feel Your Best Self and co-owner of FYBS & Co.

item.title: Repeating Words: A Developmental Phase or Something More?
item.description:
Autism

Repeating Words: A Developmental Phase or Something More?

The hidden purpose of echolalia or word and sound repetition.

Posted October 23, 2026

Key points
  • Echolalia is the repetition of words, phrases, or sentences spoken by someone else.
  • Toddlers learn language by repeating words, practicing speech, and discovering how words fit together.
  • Echolalia occurs in autism and other conditions, where repetition supports communication and self-regulation.

“Do you want a cookie?” asks a parent.

“Cookie?” echoes their toddler.

It might sound like the child is just mimicking words, but that little echo can do a lot of work. The child may be practicing new sounds, figuring out how sentences fit together, or even answering the question in the only way they know how.

We all learn language by listening and repeating, but sometimes this echoing goes beyond childhood. Known as echolalia, it can also occur in autism and other neurological or psychiatric conditions. From a toddler learning how to talk to an adult repeating a familiar phrase for comfort, echolalia reveals just how many roles repetition can play in language and communication.

From Language Learning to Repetition

Echolalia is a speech phenomenon in which a person repeats words, phrases, or sentences spoken by others. It can happen immediately, as when a child repeats a question, or later, when someone repeats words or phrases heard in the past, whether from conversations, songs, movies, or other sources.

In early childhood, echolalia is a normal part of language development. Toddlers learn by imitation, repeating words and phrases as they figure out how language works. A child might say “Time for bed!” while playing with a doll, echo “What’s that?” after hearing an adult ask the question, or recite a cartoon theme song. These repetitions help children practice pronunciation, learn sentence patterns, and gradually develop their own speech. Sometimes, echoing a question such as “Do you want a snack?” can serve as a "Yes." Echolalia is common in the first few years of life, often diminishing as children develop more fluent speech, typically by around age three (Stollznow, 2026).

However, echolalia that persists, is unusually pronounced, or occurs alongside other developmental differences may warrant closer attention. It is a recognized feature of autism spectrum disorder (ASD), although not all autistic people experience it. Some autistic children and adults use repeated phrases to communicate needs, participate in conversations, process information, or manage overwhelming situations.

Echolalia also occurs in other conditions, including Tourette syndrome, schizophrenia, epilepsy, aphasia, and other neurological disorders. In Tourette syndrome, for example, echolalia can occur as a vocal tic, involving the involuntary repetition of another person’s words. In some neurological conditions, repetition may emerge following changes in brain function. The reasons for echolalia vary, and its significance depends on the person and the context in which it's used.

When Repetition Brings Comfort

For some autistic people, echolalia serves a purpose beyond communication. Repeating familiar words or phrases can be a form of stimming, or self-soothing behavior, helping someone regulate emotions or cope with sensory overload (Camin et al., 2026). Repeating a familiar sequence of words can offer a sense of predictability and comfort when the world feels overwhelming.

Popular culture presents a memorable example in Rain Man. Dustin Hoffman’s character, Raymond Babbitt, frequently repeats familiar phrases, including “I’m an excellent driver,” and quotes lines from movies and television. When distressed, Raymond recites Abbott and Costello’s classic “Who’s on First?” routine. His reliance on familiar phrases and routines illustrates how repetition can offer comfort and predictability in overwhelming situations.

Echolalia also appears in historical accounts of Samuel Johnson, the 18th-century writer and lexicographer. Johnson displayed repetitive movements and unusual vocalizations, and some modern commentators have suggested that he may have had Tourette syndrome. He was also known to quote poetry and scripture and to talk to himself in elaborate monologues. One anecdote describes Johnson repeating a phrase spoken by his friend Hester Thrale. After he snapped at her, she responded affectionately, “Oh, dear good man!” (Roberts, 2016). Later, he was reportedly found whispering the words repeatedly to himself.

Albert Einstein has also been described as displaying echolalic speech patterns. Accounts of his childhood suggest that he sometimes repeated words and sentences quietly to himself before saying them aloud. As an adult, he reportedly repeated phrases he found amusing, sometimes saying them two or three times, particularly when excited (Andreasen, 2008).

These retrospective accounts are intriguing, but they predate modern diagnostic frameworks and cannot establish whether Johnson or Einstein actually experienced clinical echolalia.

Understanding Echolalia

Echolalia is common in early language development, but it can also persist into adulthood or occur as a feature of certain medical conditions. Understanding its significance means looking beyond the repeated words to consider the person, their circumstances, and what the repetition may be doing for them.

Echolalia reminds us that communication is not always about producing original sentences. Repeating someone else’s words can serve many functions, from learning language and communicating to processing experiences, finding comfort, or reflecting changes in how the brain works.

Rather than dismissing repetition in language as meaningless, we can recognize it as a behavior with different roles at different stages of life and in different contexts.
